title: Cannabis Social Equity Explained: Michigan's Approach
h1: What Is Cannabis Social Equity? Repairing War on Drugs Harms
metaDescription: What cannabis social equity means, why it exists, how Michigan's social equity program lowers licensing fees, and where the state's cannabis taxes go.
excerpt: Social equity programs try to repair some of the harm of past marijuana enforcement. Here is what that means, how Michigan approaches it and where cannabis tax dollars go.
keyTakeaways: Social equity programs aim to open the legal cannabis industry to people and communities hit hardest by past enforcement.
An ACLU analysis found that in 2018, Black people were 3.64 times more likely than white people to be arrested for marijuana possession, despite similar rates of use.
Michigan's Social Equity Program lowers state licensing fees for eligible applicants, such as long-term residents of 184 designated communities.
Michigan's 10% adult-use excise tax is shared with host cities and counties, K-12 schools and road repair.
body:
Cannabis social equity is the effort to make sure the people and communities most affected by marijuana prohibition share in the legal market that replaced it. In practice, that usually means help with licensing and ownership, jobs and training, and clearing old records. Michigan built a social equity program into its adult-use system, and its cannabis taxes fund schools, roads and local governments. Here's how it fits together.

## Why cannabis social equity matters: arrest disparities

For decades, marijuana enforcement fell unevenly. The ACLU's 2020 report covered arrests from 2010 to 2018. In 2018, it found, a Black person was 3.64 times more likely than a white person to be arrested for marijuana possession, up from 3.31 times in 2010. That gap held even though Black and white people use marijuana at similar rates.

The scale was large, too. In 2018 alone, the ACLU counted almost 700,000 marijuana arrests, more than 43% of all drug arrests that year. A conviction can follow someone for years after the case is closed. As states legalized, many decided that a fair legal market should include the people and neighborhoods that bore the brunt of the war on drugs.

## Three common pillars: education, employment and expungement

Equity efforts tend to rest on three pillars:

- **Education:** training and technical help so newcomers can handle licensing, compliance and running a business. A 2026 multistate analysis found that 14 of 17 states with equity licensing programs offered training.
- **Employment:** a path into ownership and jobs in the legal industry. Every one of those 17 states required equity applicants to hold majority ownership of the business.
- **Expungement:** clearing or setting aside old marijuana records, often called cannabis expungement. Our guide to [marijuana expungement in Michigan](/blog/michigan-marijuana-expungement/) explains how that works here.

## Michigan's social equity program: who qualifies and what it offers

Michigan's 2018 voter-approved law told the state's marijuana regulator, now the Cannabis Regulatory Agency (CRA), to include a plan to promote industry participation by people from communities disproportionately affected by marijuana prohibition and enforcement. The CRA's answer is its Social Equity Program, which lowers state licensing fees for eligible applicants.

According to a June 2025 summary from the Michigan Senate Fiscal Agency, applicants can qualify in three ways:

- **Residence:** at least five cumulative years in one of 184 disproportionately impacted communities identified by the CRA, for a 25% fee reduction.
- **A past marijuana conviction:** a misdemeanor brings a 25% reduction and a felony a 40% reduction. The two don't stack.
- **Caregiver history:** registration as a primary caregiver under Michigan's medical marijuana law for at least two years between 2008 and 2017.

Reductions generally combine across categories. Location matters as well. A business inside one of the designated communities gets the reduction on all its adult-use licensing fees, while one outside them gets it for two years after licensure. The designated communities are places where at least 20% of residents live below the federal poverty level, in counties with more than 660 marijuana convictions from 2008 to 2018.

The CRA has also run a Social Equity Grant Program. For the 2026 fiscal year, the state budget set aside $1 million, shared equally among adult-use licensees that are majority-owned by program participants and certified in the agency's Social Equity All-Star Program. The grants depend on the Legislature funding them each year, and program terms can change, so check the CRA's current guidance before applying.

## Equity in licensing and ownership: progress and criticism

Progress is hard to measure. A 2026 analysis by George Washington University researchers looked at 17 states that offer cannabis equity licenses or related support. The share of equity applications that led to a license ranged from 2% in Arizona to 100% in Massachusetts and Michigan.

The researchers couldn't link those outcomes clearly to how each program was designed. They suggested the programs may need more time, and better measures, before anyone can judge them.

Michigan's own figures match its high approval rate. In the 2023-24 fiscal year, the CRA received 136 applications to its Social Equity Program and approved 81 social equity license applications. None of that year's initial social equity license applications were denied, according to the Senate Fiscal Agency summary.

Approval rates don't tell the whole story, though. A lower fee doesn't cover a building, equipment or the months of costs before opening day. And in Michigan, each city, village or township can ban marijuana businesses or cap how many it allows, which narrows where any applicant, equity or not, can open a store.

## How Michigan reinvests cannabis tax revenue

Cannabis tax reinvestment in Michigan starts with a 10% excise tax on adult-use sales. Under the 2018 law, that money first covers the cost of running the program. The law also directed $20 million a year, for at least two years, to clinical trials focused on veterans. The rest is split four ways:

- **15%** to cities, villages and townships with a licensed retail store or microbusiness, in proportion to how many they host.
- **15%** to counties with those businesses, on the same basis.
- **35%** to the School Aid Fund for K-12 education.
- **35%** to the Michigan Transportation Fund for road and bridge repair.

As of October 2026, Michigan also levies a 24% wholesale tax on adult-use marijuana. The business that makes the first sale to a retailer pays it, and the revenue goes to road repair. Industry lawsuits challenging that tax were still in the courts in 2026. Neither formula sets aside a share specifically for social equity. The CRA's program relies on reduced licensing fees, plus grants in years the Legislature funds them.

## What consumers can do

If social equity matters to you, there are practical ways to act on it:

- **Learn the history.** Our articles on [Juneteenth](/blog/juneteenth/) and [Hispanic Heritage Month](/blog/hispanic-heritage-month/) look at enforcement disparities through those lenses.
- **Vote and speak up locally.** Local governments decide whether cannabis businesses can open in their communities, so local elections and public comment matter.
- **Support equity-owned businesses** where you find them.
- **Get involved.** Our guide to [cannabis advocacy organizations](/blog/cannabis-advocacy-organizations/) introduces groups working on reform and reentry.

## Where to learn more

- **The CRA** runs the Social Equity Program, so check with the agency for current terms and the list of eligible communities.
- **Our [Michigan cannabis laws guide](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/)** covers what adults 21 and older can and can't do today.
- **The ACLU's 2020 report,** A Tale of Two Countries, links to state-by-state arrest data.

faq.q: What does social equity mean in cannabis?
faq.a: It's the effort to give the people and communities most harmed by past marijuana enforcement a fair share of the legal market. Programs usually focus on three areas: help entering the industry through licensing and ownership, jobs and training, and clearing old records. The details vary widely from state to state.

faq.q: Does Michigan have a cannabis social equity program?
faq.a: Yes. The Cannabis Regulatory Agency runs a Social Equity Program that lowers state licensing fees for eligible applicants. It grew out of the 2018 voter-approved law, which told the state's regulator to plan ways to promote industry participation by people from communities disproportionately affected by marijuana prohibition. It has also offered yearly grants to licensed businesses owned by program participants when the Legislature funds them. Check the agency's current guidance for up-to-date terms.

faq.q: Who qualifies for Michigan's social equity program?
faq.a: According to a June 2025 Senate Fiscal Agency summary, there are three routes. You can qualify by living at least five cumulative years in one of 184 designated communities, or by having a past marijuana misdemeanor or felony conviction. Registered primary caregivers of at least two years between 2008 and 2017 also qualify. Published reductions are 25% for residence, 25% for a misdemeanor and 40% for a felony.

faq.q: Where does Michigan's cannabis tax money go?
faq.a: Under the 2018 law, the 10% excise tax on adult-use sales first covers program costs. The rest is split: 15% to host cities, villages and townships, 15% to host counties, 35% to K-12 schools and 35% to roads and bridges. As of October 2026, a separate 24% wholesale tax also sends its revenue to road repair.

review.notes: Legal article. Michigan social equity eligibility and the excise distribution are not in facts/law-facts.json; they rest on two Michigan Senate Fiscal Agency documents opened this session (the hard rule prefers law-facts; deviation recorded in the batch report). Nothing implies High Society is equity-licensed, funds grants or donates. No unsourced arrest numbers. Final read 2026-10-24: ACLU page, both Senate Fiscal Agency PDFs (text extracted locally) and the Chakraborty abstract re-opened; a 2026 news search shows the 15/15/35/35 split still used in the 2026 local payout. Removed "including Michigan's" (the ACLU page does not mention Michigan). Added FY2023-24 program figures from the SFA summary (136 applications received, 81 license applications approved, none denied). Added the Social Equity Grant Program (FY2026: $1 million appropriated, equal shares, adult-use licensees majority-owned by program participants and certified in the All-Star Program, subject to yearly appropriations), confirmed by a michigan.gov-only WebSearch of the CRA news release of Nov. 5, 2025 and the program FAQ (the pages themselves were not opened: michigan.gov refuses automated fetches); the benchbook source (local opt-out) was swapped for that release, since /cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/ carries the opt-out claim with its law-facts sources. DEVIATION FOR THE FACT-CHECKER: the Social Equity Program terms and the excise split are Michigan legal facts that facts/law-facts.json does not hold; they are stated from the official SFA documents, dated, with a pointer to the CRA for current terms. Fact-check 2026-10-24 (independent second pass): ACLU full report read (pdftotext), both Senate Fiscal Agency PDFs downloaded and read, Chakraborty abstract via E-utilities, law-facts for the excise, wholesale tax, litigation and local opt-out. 38 claims, 4 fixed: the ACLU 3.64 ratio is the 2018 figure (2010 was 3.31), not a 2010-2018 average (body and key takeaway); the $20 million veterans' trials line said the money "sent" (the 2018 analysis only says the law directs it); the CRA grant source was a michigan.gov URL never opened, with a path that does not match the indexed release, now the grant FAQ confirmed by search. DECISION ON THE WRITER'S FLAG: the Social Equity Program terms and the 15/15/35/35 excise split are not in law-facts; they were kept because every figure was verified this session against the two official Senate Fiscal Agency documents (same treatment as the fact-checked michigan-marijuana-expungement article), the split was confirmed still in use for the FY2025 payouts announced March 2026 (Treasury and LARA via search), and the text dates them and points to the CRA for current terms. Listed as an open issue for the orchestrator.
